name: Marketing
notes: Knowledge areas and test-item weights from the official FBLA 2025-26 Marketing guideline study guide (https://www.pafbla.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Marketing.pdf, updated November 2025; mirrors the fbla.org high school guideline): Marketing Fundamentals 10, Market Planning 10, Marketing-Information Management 15, Product/Service Management 25, Channel Management 10, Pricing 10, Promotion 10, Selling 10 test items. The objectives use MBA Research codes and include ethics in most areas, consumer protection agencies, product bundling, corporate branding and advertising media types. The event is a High School Role Play (100-question, 50-minute objective test plus interactive role play), not a case study; group is set to case as the brief requested. This bank weights the areas more evenly than the official test (fewer Product/Service Management and Marketing-Information Management items). Questions are original practice items.

questions.q: Which element of the marketing mix is most directly concerned with the amount a customer pays for a product?
questions.explain: Price is the mix variable that sets the amount a customer pays. Place covers distribution, not cost.

questions.q: A company splits a city's coffee drinkers into groups by age, income, and lifestyle, then chooses which groups to serve. Dividing the total market into groups with shared needs is called:
questions.explain: Segmentation divides the market; targeting is the later choice of which segments to serve.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the marketing concept?
choices: Maximize production volume regardless of demand
Sell whatever inventory the firm already holds
Satisfy customer needs in a way that also earns a profit
Minimize advertising spending to protect margins
questions.explain: The marketing concept treats customer needs as the route to profit.

questions.q: A manufacturer cuts unit costs and makes more units, assuming buyers will purchase whatever it produces. This reflects which business orientation?
questions.explain: A production orientation focuses on efficiency and volume. Selling orientation pushes existing goods and is the near-miss trap.

questions.q: Services are often marketed with samples, testimonials, and tangible cues because services have which characteristic?
questions.explain: Intangibility means a service cannot be inspected before purchase, so marketers add tangible cues.

questions.q: A firm sells one product with one message to the entire market. This approach is best called:
questions.explain: Undifferentiated marketing treats the whole market as one segment.

questions.q: Brand equity refers to:
choices: The cost of registering and renewing a trademark
The total revenue earned from licensing a logo
The added value a brand name gives a product beyond its features
The number of retail stores that carry the brand
questions.explain: Brand equity is the value a name adds, such as trust and recognition, beyond what the product does.

questions.q: Which of the following is a need rather than a want?
questions.explain: Needs are basic requirements; wants are specific ways of meeting needs.

questions.q: Maya realizes she needs a new laptop for school. Which stage of the consumer decision process comes first?
questions.explain: The process starts when the buyer recognizes a gap between the current and desired state.

questions.q: Which business buyer purchases goods to resell without significant change?
questions.explain: Resellers are wholesalers and retailers that buy for resale. Industrial users buy for use in production.

questions.q: A company drops a profitable product that harms the environment, weighing long-term community well-being alongside profit. Which concept does this reflect?
questions.explain: The societal marketing concept balances customer wants, company profit, and public welfare.

questions.q: Why should a firm evaluate customer lifetime value rather than the profit from one sale?
choices: It shows how quickly a store sells and replaces the inventory it holds
It removes the need to track what it costs to win each new customer
It measures how many people a single advertisement reaches in a month
It estimates total profit over the relationship to guide acquisition and retention
questions.explain: CLV estimates the total future profit from a customer, which tells the firm how much it can sensibly spend to win and keep that customer. Inventory speed and ad reach are different metrics, and CLV is used alongside acquisition cost, not instead of it.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes a marketing strategy from a marketing tactic?
choices: A strategy is the long-range plan for reaching goals; a tactic is a specific action used to carry it out
A strategy is a short-term promotional offer; a tactic is a multi-year plan
A strategy is set by sales staff; a tactic is set by finance
The two terms mean the same thing
questions.explain: Strategy is the overall plan; tactics are the specific actions that execute it.

questions.q: A firm's SWOT analysis notes a strong brand reputation. Where does this belong?
questions.explain: A brand reputation is an internal advantage, so it is a strength.

questions.q: A competitor announces it will leave the market, and the firm expects demand to shift toward it. In a SWOT, this is best classified as a(n):
questions.explain: An external factor that favors the firm is an opportunity.

questions.q: A plan states the firm will raise market share by 3 points within 12 months. This statement is a(n):
questions.explain: An objective is a measurable target with a time frame.

questions.q: Which goal best follows the SMART criteria?
choices: Increase online orders by 15% by June 30
Be the best coffee shop in town
questions.explain: SMART goals are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound.

questions.q: Market share is calculated as:
choices: Total industry sales divided by company sales
Company sales divided by total industry sales for the same period
Company profit divided by company sales
questions.explain: Market share is the firm's portion of total industry sales.

questions.q: A firm holds 12% market share in an industry with $50 million in total sales. What are the firm's sales?
questions.explain: 0.12 x $50 million = $6 million.

questions.q: Which tool plots products by market share and market growth rate?
questions.explain: The BCG matrix classifies products as stars, cash cows, question marks, or dogs.

questions.q: A product has high market share in a slow-growing market. Under the BCG matrix, it is a:
questions.explain: High share and low growth define a cash cow.

questions.q: A firm sells its existing product to new customers in a new region. Under the Ansoff matrix, this is:
questions.explain: Market development applies existing products to new markets.

questions.q: A firm lowers prices to sell more of its current product to its current customers. This Ansoff strategy is:
questions.explain: Market penetration grows existing products in existing markets.

questions.q: A firm pursues low costs but only within one narrow customer segment. Which of Porter's generic strategies is this?
questions.explain: Porter's focus strategy targets a narrow segment. Pairing it with low cost makes it a focused cost strategy.

questions.q: A firm sets its marketing budget as a fixed percentage of forecast sales. This is the:
questions.explain: The percentage-of-sales method ties the budget to sales, so it can shrink when sales fall.

questions.q: In which product life cycle stage does sales growth slow and competition intensify, pushing firms to differentiate?
questions.explain: Maturity is when growth flattens and competition is strongest.

questions.q: In a PESTEL analysis, a new federal rule restricting how sugar content can be labeled falls under which factor?
questions.explain: A regulation is a political-legal factor.

questions.q: Data that already exists from another source, such as census figures, is called:
questions.explain: Secondary data was collected for another purpose. Primary data is gathered firsthand.

questions.q: A company surveys 500 customers with a standardized questionnaire to measure satisfaction numerically. This is:
questions.explain: Standardized, numerical, firsthand survey data is quantitative primary research.

questions.q: A moderator leads eight consumers through an open discussion of a new snack. This is a:
questions.explain: A focus group is a small moderated discussion aimed at qualitative insight.

questions.q: Which sampling method gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection?
questions.explain: Simple random sampling gives each member an equal probability of selection.

questions.q: A marketer compares sales at two stores, one with a new display and one without, holding other factors constant. This is:
questions.explain: Changing one variable against a comparison group while controlling the rest is an experiment.

questions.q: An online retailer analyzes purchase histories to predict what customers will buy next. This is best described as:
questions.explain: Data mining finds patterns in large databases to support predictions.

questions.q: A survey gives the same results when repeated under the same conditions. This describes which research quality?
questions.explain: Reliability means consistent results across repeated measurements.

questions.q: A survey asks, 'Don't you agree our fresh menu is far better than competitors?' Which problem most affects the results?
questions.explain: The wording pushes respondents toward one answer, which is leading question bias.

questions.q: A firm must choose between a $500 secondary-data review and a $25,000 primary survey. Which factor best supports starting with secondary research?
choices: Secondary data is always more current than primary data
Secondary data is collected to answer the firm's exact question
Secondary data gives the firm insight competitors cannot access
Secondary data is cheaper and faster for a first look at the problem
questions.explain: Secondary research is a low-cost, quick first step. It is often dated, was gathered for someone else's purpose and is open to competitors too, which is why primary research may still be needed afterwards.

questions.q: Which metric asks customers how likely they are to recommend a brand?
questions.explain: Net Promoter Score is built on a likelihood-to-recommend question.

questions.q: A marketing team wants to know whether a new ad caused awareness to rise. Which design best isolates the ad's effect?
choices: A survey after the campaign of only the people who saw the ad
Before-and-after awareness surveys of exposed and unexposed groups
A count of total website visits during the weeks the ad ran
A focus group asking viewers whether they liked the ad's message
questions.explain: Measuring awareness before and after in both an exposed group and an unexposed comparison group separates the ad's effect from other causes. A post-only survey has no baseline, and web visits or liking the ad do not show that the ad caused the change.

questions.q: Brand positioning is best defined as:
choices: The legal registration of a brand name
The number of licenses a firm holds on its brand
The place a brand holds in customers' minds relative to competitors
The cost of a brand's advertising
questions.explain: Positioning is the perceived place of a brand relative to rivals.

questions.q: A product's core benefit is best described as:
choices: The look and material of its packaging
The warranty and service that come with it
The brand name and features buyers see
The fundamental need the product satisfies
questions.explain: The core benefit is the problem the product solves for the buyer. Brand name and features are the actual product, and warranty and service are the augmented product.

questions.q: A company sells a basic phone and a premium phone, built on the same platform and sold as one family of related models. This is best described as:
questions.explain: A product line is a group of related products; managing the lines within the mix is product line management.

questions.q: In new product development, which stage tests the product idea with target customers before full development?
questions.explain: Concept testing gauges target customers' reaction to the idea.

questions.q: A sportswear brand uses its name on a new line of kitchen appliances. This is a:
questions.explain: Brand extension uses an established name in a different product category.

questions.q: A soup company adds a new flavor to its existing soup line. This is a:
questions.explain: A line extension adds items within the same category.

questions.q: The sequence of introduction, growth, maturity, and decline describes the:
questions.explain: Those four stages make up the product life cycle.

questions.q: In the diffusion of innovations, which adopter group tries new products first?
questions.explain: Innovators are the first group to adopt a new product.

questions.q: A firm drops a product with falling sales, high costs, and a negative contribution margin. This is:
questions.explain: Pruning removes weak products from the product mix.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of a consistent brand identity?
choices: It eliminates the need for quality control
It lowers the price customers will pay
It makes a brand easier to recognize and recall
questions.explain: Consistency builds recognition and recall.

questions.q: Which packaging function is mainly about keeping the product safe while it is shipped and stored?
questions.explain: Protection is the packaging function for transport and storage.

questions.q: In the United States, which legal instrument primarily protects a brand's name, logo, and tagline?
questions.explain: Trademarks protect brand identifiers. Patents cover inventions and copyrights cover creative works.

questions.q: Intermediaries that take title to goods and resell them to retailers are called:
questions.explain: Wholesalers take title and resell, typically to retailers or business users.

questions.q: A manufacturer sells directly to consumers through its own website. This is a:
questions.explain: No intermediaries are used, so it is a direct channel.

questions.q: Intensive distribution means the product is sold in:
questions.explain: Intensive distribution maximizes outlets, which suits convenience goods.

questions.q: A luxury watch brand grants one authorized jeweler sole rights to sell its watches in each city. Which distribution strategy is this?
questions.explain: Exclusive distribution gives a limited number of dealers sole rights in a territory.

questions.q: A manufacturer sells directly online at prices below its retail partners, causing friction with them. This is:
choices: Supplier conflict over raw material costs
questions.explain: Multichannel conflict arises when a producer's direct channel competes with its existing channels.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an agent from a broker?
choices: An agent takes title to the goods; a broker does not
Both take title to the goods they help sell
A broker works only for sellers; an agent works only for buyers
An agent has a lasting client relationship; a broker arranges one-off deals
questions.explain: Neither agents nor brokers take title. Agents represent buyers or sellers on a more lasting basis, while brokers bring parties together for a single transaction and assist in negotiation. Either can work for buyers or sellers.

questions.q: Which channel function means a retailer holds goods so they are available when customers want them?
questions.explain: Storage and inventory holding keeps goods on hand for customers.

questions.q: A firm removes an intermediary and sells straight to customers. This is called:
questions.explain: Disintermediation removes middlemen from a channel.

questions.q: A company's outlets are run by independent operators under a contract that sets the business model. This is a:
questions.explain: A franchise is a contractual vertical marketing system.

questions.q: A retailer's inventory turnover ratio is calculated as:
choices: Average inventory divided by cost of goods sold
Gross profit divided by net sales
Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory
questions.explain: Turnover uses cost of goods sold over average inventory at cost.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of using a wholesaler?
choices: It reduces the number of contacts a manufacturer must make with retailers
It gives the manufacturer more control over how retailers display the product
It lets the manufacturer keep the wholesaler's margin as extra profit
It shortens the channel between the manufacturer and the consumer
questions.explain: A wholesaler lets a manufacturer reach many retailers through one contact, cutting the number of transactions. Adding a wholesaler lengthens the channel and usually reduces the maker's control and share of the margin.

questions.q: A firm sets price by adding a fixed percentage to its unit cost. This is:
questions.explain: Cost-plus pricing adds a markup to cost.

questions.q: A new high-tech product launches at a high price, which is lowered over time. This describes:
questions.explain: Skimming starts high and steps down to reach successive groups of buyers.

questions.q: A product costs $20 per unit, and the firm applies a 25% markup on cost. What is the selling price?
A retailer sells an item for $80 that cost $48. What is the gross margin percentage based on selling price?
Fixed costs are $12,000 per month. Price is $30 and variable cost is $18 per unit. How many units break even?
Which approach sets a low introductory price to gain market share quickly?
questions.explain: Penetration pricing starts low to win share.

questions.q: Prices such as $9.99 are an example of:
questions.explain: Odd-even pricing uses prices ending in odd numbers to appear lower.

questions.q: If demand for a product is elastic, a 10% price increase will most likely cause:
choices: Quantity demanded to fall by more than 10%
Quantity demanded to fall by less than 10%
questions.explain: Elastic demand means quantity falls by a larger percentage than price rises.

questions.q: A retailer discounts a printer and earns profit on the ink cartridges buyers must purchase. This is:
questions.explain: Captive product pricing discounts the base product and earns on required supplies.

questions.q: A business sets its price at the level competitors charge for similar products. This is:
questions.explain: Going-rate pricing follows the prevailing market rate.

questions.q: What is the main risk of relying on cost-based pricing alone?
choices: It requires detailed data on competitors' costs
It cannot be used by retailers or wholesalers
It forces prices to change every time demand shifts
It ignores customer demand and the value customers perceive
questions.explain: Cost-based pricing looks only at the firm's own costs, so it can set prices above what customers will pay or below the value they see. It needs only internal cost data, retailers use it widely through markups, and it does not react to demand at all.

questions.q: A product sells for $40 with a variable cost of $25 per unit. What is its contribution margin per unit?
questions.explain: $40 - $25 = $15 per unit toward fixed costs.

questions.q: A firm offers a product in three versions at $19, $29, and $39. What is the main purpose of this price lining?
choices: To raise prices across all products
To simplify choices across defined quality tiers
questions.explain: Price lining sets clear tiers for the customer to choose from.

questions.q: Which promotional mix element is paid, nonpersonal communication from an identified sponsor?
questions.explain: Advertising is paid and nonpersonal, with an identified sponsor.

questions.q: Free news coverage of a company's new product is:
questions.explain: Publicity is unpaid media coverage.

questions.q: A coupon giving 20% off the next purchase is an example of:
questions.explain: Sales promotions are short-term incentives.

questions.q: In the AIDA model, which stage requires the ad to create a strong wish to own the product?
questions.explain: Desire follows interest and builds the want to own.

questions.q: In the AIDA model, which stage aims to get the consumer to buy now?
questions.explain: Action is the final stage.

questions.q: Which promotional mix element has a company's salespeople presenting directly to buyers?
questions.explain: Personal selling is two-way and direct.

questions.q: A brand decides to reach 18 to 24-year-olds through influencer posts on one platform. This choice is most directly a:
questions.explain: Choosing the medium and vehicle to reach an audience is a media selection decision.

questions.q: An email offering loyalty rewards to customers who purchased in the past year is an example of:
questions.explain: Direct marketing targets known customers to prompt a response.

questions.q: A media plan says the average consumer will see an ad three times. This measure is:
questions.explain: Frequency counts repeated exposures per person.

questions.q: An ad campaign costs $12,000 and reaches 2,000,000 people. What is its cost per thousand (CPM)?
questions.explain: $12,000 / 2,000 thousand people = $6.00.

questions.q: A 'buy one, get one free' offer is mainly used to:
questions.explain: Sales promotions drive short-term action.

questions.q: A store advertises a TV at a very low price but stocks almost none, then steers shoppers who ask for it toward a pricier model. This deceptive practice is called:
questions.explain: Bait and switch advertises an item the seller does not really intend to sell in order to push a costlier one, which the FTC treats as deceptive advertising. A loss leader is a real low-priced item the store actually sells to draw traffic.

questions.q: Public relations primarily helps a firm by:
choices: Guaranteeing a set level of sales volume
Setting prices for the firm's products
Managing its image and relationships with stakeholders
questions.explain: Public relations manages image and stakeholder relationships.

questions.q: Identifying qualified potential customers is which selling step?
questions.explain: Prospecting finds and qualifies leads.

questions.q: A salesperson asks open-ended questions to learn needs before presenting. This is:
questions.explain: Needs assessment uncovers the buyer's problems.

questions.q: A customer says, 'Your price is higher than a competitor's.' What is the best response?
choices: Offer to match the competitor's price before asking any questions
Acknowledge the concern and explain value and total cost of ownership
Point out every weakness of the competitor's product in detail
Repeat the price and move straight to asking for the order
questions.explain: Acknowledging the objection and then showing value (quality, service, total cost) answers the real concern. Matching the price at once gives away margin, attacking the competitor hurts credibility, and skipping past the objection leaves it unresolved.

questions.q: Which closing technique offers two options, both of which lead to a sale?
questions.explain: The alternative choice close offers two acceptable paths to a sale.

questions.q: A rep sends a thank-you note two days after a purchase. This is which step?
questions.explain: Follow-up supports retention after the sale.

questions.q: Which selling approach aims at a long-term partnership rather than one transaction?
questions.explain: Relationship selling builds ongoing trust.

questions.q: A rep's commission rate rises once sales exceed a set level. This is a(n):
questions.explain: Accelerated plans raise the commission rate above a threshold.

questions.q: Which behavior is consultative selling?
choices: Offering the same discount to every buyer
Asking diagnostic questions and tailoring the solution
questions.explain: Consultative selling diagnoses needs before recommending.

questions.q: A manager tracks calls made per week to evaluate a rep. This is a:
questions.explain: Activity metrics such as calls made predict future sales.

questions.q: What is the best use of a trial close?
choices: To check the customer's readiness to buy before the final close
To end the sales call once the customer raises an objection
To offer a lower price before the customer asks for one
To skip the presentation and go straight to the order form
questions.explain: A trial close tests readiness before asking for the order.

questions.q: How should customer objections be viewed?
choices: Signals of rejection that mean the sale is over
Requests for information and reassurance that can advance the sale
Reasons to hand the customer to a different salesperson
Arguments the salesperson must win before closing
questions.explain: Objections are openings to clarify value and move the sale forward.

questions.q: A rep learns that the buyer's purchase must be approved by a buying committee. What is the rep's best next step?
choices: Push the current contact to sign before the committee meets
Offer a deep discount so the committee approves quickly
Ask who else influences the decision and map the buying group
Send the same proposal to the committee and wait for a reply
questions.explain: In a committee purchase the rep needs to know every influencer and decision maker and what each one cares about. Pressuring one contact, discounting early, or sending a generic proposal ignores the people who actually decide.

questions.q: A sales manager divides each rep's closed deals by the number of qualified leads the rep worked. Which metric is the manager calculating?
questions.explain: Conversion (close) rate is closed deals divided by leads or opportunities worked. Gross margin measures profitability, days sales outstanding measures collection speed, and inventory turnover measures how fast stock sells.

vocab.def: A business philosophy holding that satisfying customer needs at a profit is the route to organizational goals.
Dividing a broad market into groups of buyers who share similar needs or characteristics.
The controllable product, price, place, and promotion variables a firm combines to serve a target market.
A basic requirement for survival or well-being, such as food, water, or shelter.
A desire for a specific way of satisfying a need, shaped by culture and personality.
The added value a brand name gives a product beyond its functional features.
The sequence of problem recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase, and post-purchase evaluation.
A review of internal strengths and weaknesses together with external opportunities and threats.
A measurable target a marketing plan aims to reach within a set time frame.
A firm's sales as a percentage of total industry sales for a product over a period.
A portfolio tool that classifies products as stars, cash cows, question marks, or dogs by market share and market growth.
A product with high market share in a slow-growing market that generates more cash than it needs.
A growth framework with four strategies: market penetration, market development, product development, and diversification.
Growth by selling more of existing products in existing markets.
A scan of the political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal forces in the external environment.
Data collected firsthand for the specific study at hand.
Analysis of data that was already collected for another purpose.
A small, moderated discussion used to gather qualitative consumer opinions.
A sampling method in which every member of the population has an equal chance of selection.
A structured process for gathering, sorting, analyzing, and distributing information for marketing decisions.
The degree to which a measurement gives consistent results when repeated under the same conditions.
The degree to which a research instrument measures what it was designed to measure.
A group of closely related products that are sold to the same customer groups or work in similar ways.
Using an established brand name for a new product in a different product category.
Adding new items within the same product category under an existing brand.
The place a brand occupies in customers' minds relative to competing brands.
The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
The process by which a new product or idea spreads through a population over time.
A word, name, symbol, or design that identifies a seller's goods and is legally protected against use by others; in the U.S. it can be registered with the USPTO.
An intermediary that buys and takes title to goods, then resells them mainly to retailers or business users.
An intermediary that represents a buyer or seller on an ongoing basis and typically does not take title to goods.
Placing a product in as many outlets as possible.
Granting a limited number of dealers sole rights to sell a product in a territory.
Using a moderate number of carefully chosen outlets in a market.
Disagreement among channel members over goals, roles, prices, or territory.
Removing intermediaries from a channel so the producer sells more directly to customers.
A channel in which producers, wholesalers, and retailers act as one coordinated system.
The ratio of cost of goods sold to average inventory, showing how often stock is sold and replaced.
Setting a price by adding a markup to the cost of producing a product.
Starting with a high price and lowering it over time to capture successive layers of demand.
Setting a low initial price to gain market share quickly.
The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price.
The sales volume at which total revenue equals total costs.
Selling price minus variable cost per unit, the amount each unit contributes toward fixed costs.
A product sold at or below cost to attract customers who buy other items.
A low price on a core product with profit earned on the supplies that product requires.
Paid, nonpersonal communication from an identified sponsor.
Unpaid media coverage of a company, product, or idea.
A short-term incentive that encourages purchase or trial, such as coupons or rebates.
Two-way, direct communication between a salesperson and a buyer.
The attention, interest, desire, and action stages a promotion aims to move a consumer through.
The number of unique people or households exposed to a message in a period.
The average number of times a person is exposed to a message in a period.
The cost of delivering an advertisement to 1,000 people.
Identifying and qualifying potential customers.
A questioning process that uncovers a buyer's needs and problems before a solution is offered.
A customer concern or resistance raised during a sale that must be addressed.
A question that tests a buyer's readiness to purchase before the final close.
An approach in which the salesperson diagnoses needs and tailors solutions as a trusted advisor.
A focus on long-term customer partnerships rather than a single transaction.
